content.content:
1	# The report and the record
     2	
     3	## What every report holds
     4	
     5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
     6	
     7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
     8	
     9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
    10	
    11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
    12	
    13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
    14	
    15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
    16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
    17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
    18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
    19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
    20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
    21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
    22	
    23	## At a point to report
    24	
    25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
    26	- Then finish the work.
    27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
    28	
    29	## Timings and citations
    30	
    31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
    32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
    33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
    34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
    35	
    36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
    37	
    38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
    39	
    40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
    41	
    42	## The gap ledger
    43	
    44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
    45	
    46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
    47	
    48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
    49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
    50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
    51	
    52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
    53	
    54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
    55	
    56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
    57	
    58	## Reading the record
    59	
    60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
    61	
    62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
    63	
    64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
    65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
    66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
    67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
    68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
    69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
    70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
    71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
    72	
    73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
    74	
    75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
    76	
    77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
    78	
    79	## Writing to the record
    80	
    81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
    82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
    83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
    84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
    85	  - what it means for the work;
    86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
    87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
    88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
    89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
    90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
    91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
    92	
    93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
    94	
    95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
    96	
    97	To add a row:
    98	
    99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
   100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
   101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
   102	
   103	To change a row:
   104	
   105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no note.
   106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
   107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
   108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
   109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem that the commits after BASE leave in the record, and exits 1 on any. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
   110	
   111	## The repository's history
   112	
   113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
   114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
   115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
   116	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
   117	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
   118	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

content.content:
1	---
     2	name: coordinator
     3	description: "Use this skill in the Fortress revival's coordinating session whenever the curator (who decides what is committed and what agents do) is directing you, waiting on you, or setting how the conversation goes. Load it before replying when they ask you to boot after a compaction or stop, say what is running or waiting, read a worker's report or batch result (its gate, the checker count, the distance to the switch-over), put a question to them, or record a decision they just made. Load it too when they say they will review your turns one by one, ask you to hold or restate something, keep quiet during a batch, or change your register or format. Load it before briefing, launching, resuming or relaunching agents, picking a tier, estimating tokens, or editing FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, the review queue, boot note or held list. Not for workers, build/test work (fortress-repo), container or hook faults (cloud-container), or generic multi-agent or ADR questions."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# The coordinating session
     7	
     8	You talk to the curator, brief the workers and keep the record. Load a part under `references/` when you switch into its work.
     9	
    10	**curator**
    11	: Person in charge of this restoration.
    12	
    13	**worker**
    14	: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.
    15	
    16	**record**
    17	: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that the core lists below.
    18	
    19	**entry**
    20	: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.
    21	
    22	**PLAN**
    23	: Working plan, `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`. Its last phases are 3, the checker at zero; 4, the switch-over; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. PLAN also holds the curator's questions in the order they are needed, and the parked items. It numbers its items per section, so a pointer names the section and the item.
    24	
    25	**review queue**
    26	: `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`: numbered items that wait for the curator's word or review. A pointer cites an item by its number.
    27	
    28	**default**
    29	: Choice that an agent made and landed without the curator's word. It stands in the tree, and its item in the review queue waits for the curator's review.
    30	
    31	**batch**
    32	: Run of the batch workflow (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.
    33	
    34	**rung**
    35	: One task of a batch, with its own worker and worktree. Its brief is its section of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`.
    36	
    37	**fork**
    38	: Design question with more than one way forward.
    39	
    40	**cross-area question**
    41	: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.
    42	
    43	**go**
    44	: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.
    45	
    46	**ask**
    47	: Message that puts one decision to the curator.
    48	
    49	**hold**
    50	: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.
    51	
    52	**review list**
    53	: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: items for the curator's later review.
    54	
    55	**interrupt**
    56	: Stop of a turn by the stop button.
    57	
    58	**process stop**
    59	: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.
    60	
    61	**tokens written**
    62	: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.
    63	
    64	**boot note**
    65	: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.
    66	
    67	**held list**
    68	: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.
    69	
    70	**model check**
    71	: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.
    72	
    73	**git-check switch**
    74	: Hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.
    75	
    76	## The standing goal
    77	
    78	You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.
    79	
    80	- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
    81	- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
    82	- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.
    83	
    84	## The curator's role and decisions
    85	
    86	The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
    87	
    88	Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
    89	
    90	A decision is consequential if it:
    91	
    92	- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
    93	- touches microGPT: a line of the model program, its speed or its readability;
    94	- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
    95	- or cannot be undone.
    96	
    97	It reaches the curator in one of three ways:
    98	
    99	1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
   100	2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
   101	3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.
   102	
   103	Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.
   104	
   105	- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
   106	- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
   107	- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
   108	- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
   109	- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
   110	- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
   111	- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
   112	- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
   113	- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
   114	- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.
   115	
   116	## The facts of this environment
   117	
   118	- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
   119	- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
   120	- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
   121	- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
   122	- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
   123	- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
   124	- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
   125	- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
   126	- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
   127	- The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part). Its reminders are advisory. If a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn: answer it as "Quiet times" says.
   128	- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
   129	- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
   130	- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.
   131	
   132	## Talking to the curator
   133	
   134	- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
   135	- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
   136	- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
   137	- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
   138	- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
   139	- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
   140	- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
   141	- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
   142	- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
   143	- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
   144	- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
   145	- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.
   146	
   147	**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:
   148	
   149	1. The question, in one line.
   150	2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
   151	3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
   152	4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
   153	5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
   154	
   155	Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.
   156	
   157	Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
   158	
   159	**Quiet times.**
   160	
   161	- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
   162	  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
   163	  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.
   164	
   165	  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.

1	# Running and reviewing a batch
     2	
     3	The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.
     4	
     5	**batch record**
     6	: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<name>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.
     7	
     8	**base**
     9	: Commit that the batch starts from.
    10	
    11	**gather**
    12	: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.
    13	
    14	**merged-diff review**
    15	: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.
    16	
    17	**repair round**
    18	: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.
    19	
    20	**commit stage**
    21	: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.
    22	
    23	**reserved point**
    24	: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.
    25	
    26	**checker count**
    27	: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.
    28	
    29	**distance**
    30	: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.
    31	
    32	## The go
    33	
    34	- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
    35	- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
    36	- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.
    37	
    38	## The workflow
    39	
    40	- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
    41	- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
    42	- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
    43	- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
    44	- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
    45	- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.
    46	
    47	## The roles
    48	
    49	- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
    50	- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
    51	- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
    52	- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.
    53	
    54	## The checker count and the distance
    55	
    56	The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.
    57	
    58	- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
    59	- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
    60	- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
    61	- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.
    62	
    63	## Reserved points and repairs
    64	
    65	- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
    66	- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
    67	- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
    68	- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
    69	- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.
    70	
    71	## While it runs
    72	
    73	- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
    74	- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Push nothing to `main` from any tree, or git refuses the landing's push.
    75	- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
    76	- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
    77	- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.
    78	
    79	## The landing
    80	
    81	The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. Any finding fails the stage until it is cleared through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or the entry is reworded. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.
    82	
    83	If the batch's push is held for the curator, take the steps below at once on the local commits. Only the push waits, and the parts of the routing that need the pushed hashes.
    84	
    85	1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
    86	2. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
    87	3. Run the orientation workflow in update mode on the landing's new and changed FACTS entries, and have the writer install its result (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
    88	4. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
    89	5. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
    90	6. File what the review finds in PLAN. Then make these moves yourself. The manual's section "After the landing: the coordinator's routing" gives `PLAN-history.md`'s heading for each landing and the form of the one line.
    91	   - Move word for word into `PLAN-history.md` each item that the batch built, each question that the batch or the curator answered, and each stale item. A stale item is one that a decision or a landed change has made moot.
    92	   - If another home holds an open item's whole text, cut it in PLAN to one line with a pointer there. If it holds part, first move the rest there. This holds for the review lists too: an entry that `review-queue.md` holds becomes such a line.
    93	   - Repoint each citation of a moved item: `git grep -n 'PLAN\.md' -- explorations/coordinator/*.md explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md .claude/skills`.

1	# Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming workers
     2	
     3	**Workflow run**
     4	: Run of a script by the Workflow tool, which launches one agent for each `agent()` call.
     5	
     6	**journal**
     7	: Workflow run's log, `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line for each agent call and a `result` line with its structured result.
     8	
     9	**headless session**
    10	: `claude -p` session started from your shell.
    11	
    12	**archaeology**
    13	: Search of git and the transcripts for how something came about. It returns cited evidence, not a judgement.
    14	
    15	**writer stream**
    16	: Headless Opus session that writes the chunks of a long writing pass in turn, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`.
    17	
    18	## Which tier runs what
    19	
    20	- Give each worker its tier's alias: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`. Write no identifier that an alias resolves to.
    21	- Use Sonnet for archaeology and retrieval only, never for a judgement.
    22	- Run every writer on Opus: of skill text, of record entries, and of each longer report or page for the curator, also when this session runs on Fable. The curator dislikes Fable's register.
    23	- Take a cross-area question in two steps. First, Opus workers gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if neither the record nor the three principles (`SKILL.md`) settle it, run a Fable judgement, sparingly. If the fork stays consequential, put it to the curator as an ask.
    24	- Four kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: the Fable judgement on a cross-area question, a judge's second ruling in a batch, the Fable review of each batch record, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
    25	- If you start a headless session on a tier other than Opus or Fable, set `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment. Otherwise the model check's alarm stops its work (`SKILL.md`, "The boot"). Today only the baseline interview does so.
    26	- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.
    27	
    28	## What a brief holds
    29	
    30	- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
    31	- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
    32	- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
    33	- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
    34	- The entries that it needs, quoted word for word under their numbers. Quote a rule of the curator's whole, with its limit and its example.
    35	- Before you quote the curator's words from a message, clean them. Fix the obvious typos of the phone's swipe keyboard and of dictation, and keep the meaning. Put `[?]` after each word whose reading is a guess. Quote an entry as the record holds it.
    36	- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
    37	- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
    38	- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
    39	- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 270 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.
    40	
    41	A worker whose task touches the repository loads `fortress-repo` by itself. That skill tells it which choices are its own.
    42	
    43	## Watching a run
    44	
    45	- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
    46	- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
    47	- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
    48	- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
    49	- If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).
    50	
    51	## Interrupts and process stops
    52	
    53	An interrupt or a process stop kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.
    54	
    55	- After an accidental interrupt, tell the curator, and resume the run.
    56	- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
    57	- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A hash given short where the launch gave it in full misses from the first call.
    58	- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched: `git show <launch commit>:<path>`. If the call order would differ, wrap `agent()` in the copy, so that the finished calls come in the journal's order of `started` lines. `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md` has such a wrapper (`resumeOrder`).
    59	- If a batch's commit stage was killed before it committed, its edits are in `/home/user/fortress`. Resume with a commit prompt that names them.
    60	- If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, `git stash` its staged changes and keep the stash before you resume.
    61	- A new session cannot resume another session's run.
    62	- An Agent-tool worker that a process stop killed goes on from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. One that an interrupt killed cannot. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask, and tell the new worker its predecessor's leftovers.
    63	- Give a Fable successor the leftovers in the tree, never the transcript: the safety filter can end a Fable worker that prints one.
    64	
    65	## The Workflow tool
    66	
    67	- The tool runs at most two agents at once on this machine. The others wait.
    68	- Across agents, the cache serves the first message only when the whole prompt is identical. A project agent type's system prompt is cached for every agent of the type, so put text that every agent needs there.
    69	- A project agent type written during the session is found only after a process stop. A project skill appears at once.
    70	- `agent()` can return null for an agent that the harness marks failed after it delivered its result. Read its branch before you run it again.
    71	- Check a script by parsing it as an async function body, not with `node --check`: `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js`.
    72	
    73	## A long writing pass
    74	
    75	Run a long writing pass, such as a run of the clarity or orientation workflow, as writer streams.
    76	
    77	- The script resumes a stream while its context is small and its prompt cache is warm. Its header gives the limits. Otherwise it starts a fresh session.
    78	- So a fix round resumes the session that wrote the text, with its evidence still in the cache. A fresh writer would read everything again.
    79	- Give each Workflow run its own stream, and run several side by side.
    80	- End each round with one judge, which applies or holds each chunk's items. No chunk goes through a second fix round.
    81	
    82	## A second session
    83	
    84	A second coordinating session contributes reviews and their commits, on a branch of its own from `main`. It runs no batch and does not change PLAN's order.

 ## What an entry is
 
-An entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
-
-- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
-- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what it means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.
+An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
+
+- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
+- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.

PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
+- If the tree lacks a part of a decision or a fact, that part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
+- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
+- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
 - Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
 - A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
 - An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
@@ -33,6 +37,24 @@ Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
 5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
 6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
 
+Judge a FACTS entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail or unresolved, and quote the passage that fails:
+
+- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
+- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
+- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim.
+- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
+- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
+- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
+
+A fail of scope, evidence or consistency blocks the entry. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
+
+- keep: every check passes;
+- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
+- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
+- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording.
+
+The detail of each check is in `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`, "Per-entry assessment rubric".
+

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

"""skills-lint.py [FILE...]: find the coordinator's agenda in the project skills.
